chapters.title: Chapter 3: Pulling the Three Working Capital Levers

lessons.title: Managing Payables: Paying Suppliers Smartly and the MSME 45-Day Rule

children.text: Payables are the one part of working capital that funds you instead of draining you. Every day a supplier waits is a day you do not need a bank. That makes payables tempting to stretch, and stretching is exactly where Indian businesses get into trouble, because the law now puts a hard floor under how long you may take with your smallest suppliers. This lesson is about using supplier credit properly and knowing precisely where the floor is.

body.text: Supplier credit is the cheapest funding a business will ever get, and the most expensive to abuse. The question is never how long can we delay, it is which supplier, on what agreed terms, and at what cost in price, priority and law.

children.text: Three Very Different Piles of Money
Before touching payment timing, split what you owe into three categories. They behave nothing alike.

body.caption: What you owe, and what you may do about it

cells: TDS, GST, PF, ESI, advance tax
Never. Interest and penalties apply automatically, and in some cases personal liability follows
Local fabricators, packaging units, job workers registered on Udyam
Only within the statutory limit. Beyond it there is compound interest and a tax cost
Yes, by negotiation and in writing. Never unilaterally

body.text: Unilateral stretching is not a strategy, it is a default with better manners. The supplier notices immediately, and the price of your next purchase order quietly goes up to cover it. Negotiated terms are permanent. Silent delays are borrowed twice, once in cash and once in your reputation.

children.text: The Rule That Sets the Floor

Under Section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006, a buyer must pay a micro or small supplier within the agreed period, which cannot exceed 45 days from acceptance, or within 15 days if there is no written agreement. Miss it and three separate consequences follow, and most managers know about only one.
Compound interest, Section 16 of the MSMED Act.
Three times the RBI bank rate, compounded with monthly rests, running from the appointed day. It is payable whether or not the supplier asks for it.
That interest is not tax deductible, Section 23 of the MSMED Act.
The cost is borne in full, with no tax relief to soften it.
The purchase itself stops being deductible until paid,

under Section 37(2)(g) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, the provision that carried over from Section 43B(h) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. If the amount is unpaid past the limit at the year end, the deduction moves to the year you actually pay.

body.title: What those three penalties cost on ₹40 lakh

children.text: Take a buyer who owes ₹40 lakh to micro and small suppliers, unpaid past the statutory limit on 31 March.
The deduction is deferred.

₹40 lakh of cost is added back to this year's taxable profit. At an effective tax rate of about 25%, that is roughly ₹10 lakh of extra tax paid this year, recovered only when the supplier is actually paid.
Interest accrues.
If the RBI bank rate were 6%, three times that is 18% a year, and with monthly rests the effective rate is about 19.6%.
The interest gets no tax relief.
Section 23 denies the deduction, so every rupee of it comes out of post-tax money.

Cash-wise, the business has pushed ₹40 lakh of payment into the future and pulled ₹10 lakh of tax into the present, while accruing interest at close to 20%. Delaying a small supplier is one of the most expensive forms of finance available in India today.

One caution on scope: the provision applies to micro and small enterprises, not medium ones, and its application to traders has been a contested area. Confirm the position with your chartered accountant for your own vendor base.

body.label: Companies must also report the delay
body.context: A company that owes a micro or small supplier for more than 45 days files MSME Form 1 with the Registrar of Companies, by 31 October for the April to September half-year and by 30 April for October to March. The delay is not just expensive, it is on a public file.

body.title: Which suppliers are covered
body.textWithBlank: The MSMED 45-day payment rule and the related tax disallowance apply to micro and ___ enterprises.
body.explanation: Micro and small only. Medium enterprises are outside both the 45-day protection in practice for these purposes and the tax disallowance. This is exactly why the vendor master must record each supplier's Udyam classification, not just the fact that they have a Udyam number.

body.title: Clean up your vendor master this quarter
steps: Ask every supplier for their Udyam registration number and their classification: micro, small or medium.
Record the classification as a field in the vendor master, not as a note in an email.
Tag invoices from micro and small suppliers automatically, so payment terms default to the statutory limit.
Get the written agreement in place where terms are agreed, because without one the limit drops to 15 days.
Run an exception report every month for micro and small invoices approaching 40 days.
Reconcile that report with what the accounts team will have to disclose in MSME Form 1 and in the notes to the accounts.
Ask suppliers to refresh their Udyam status annually, since classification changes as they grow.

children.text: Where Real Negotiation Happens
With the floor established, the room to manoeuvre is with large suppliers, and it is genuine. Konkan Ceramics buys ₹8.4 crore a year. Here is how that splits.

body.title: Konkan Ceramics: annual purchases by supplier type (₹ crore)

children.text: About 55% of purchases come from micro and small suppliers, so more than half the payables book has a legal floor under it. The company decides to get compliant and pay for it by negotiating with the one large supplier it has.

body.caption: The rebalancing plan, in cash terms

cells: Pay micro and small suppliers in 45 days instead of 60
Negotiate glaze supplier from 45 to 75 days
Releases ₹2.5 lakh, and the company is compliant

body.text: This is the shape of a realistic payables plan. Compliance with the small suppliers costs cash, and that cost is funded by negotiating properly with a large one who can absorb it and who will price the terms openly. The business ends up lawful, better funded and with suppliers who actually want its orders.

body.title: What to offer a large supplier for longer terms

columns.label: Things that genuinely buy you days
points: Committed annual volumes with a rolling forecast
Fewer, larger orders that cut their handling cost
Reliable payment on the agreed date, every single time
A letter of credit or a bank guarantee backing the exposure
Supply chain finance, where your bank pays them early at your credit rating

columns.label: Things that cost you more than they save
points: Simply paying late and waiting to be asked
Disputing invoices to delay a payment run
Agreeing terms verbally that finance then ignores
Taking 90 days from a supplier who funds it at 18%, then facing a price rise
Stretching a supplier who is your only source for a critical input

body.title: Supply chain finance, the option that suits both sides

children.text: Also called reverse factoring, this is the mirror image of the TReDS transaction from Lesson 3.1, arranged by the buyer rather than the supplier.
You approve the supplier's invoice on a bank platform.
The bank pays the supplier immediately, discounting at a rate based on your credit rating, which is usually far better than theirs.
You pay the bank on the extended due date.

The supplier gets cash in days, you keep or extend your terms, and the funding is priced off the stronger balance sheet in the relationship. For a buyer with a good rating and many small suppliers, this often solves the entire tension in this lesson at once. Two cautions: check how the arrangement is classified in your accounts, since heavy use can look like borrowing, and confirm with your adviser how paying through such a programme sits against the MSMED timeline.

body.title: Should you take the discount?
body.prompt: A large supplier offers 2% off if you pay within 10 days instead of the agreed 45 days, so you pay 35 days sooner. What is the annualised return on using your cash that way, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 2 divided by 98 is 0.0204, and 365 divided by 35 is 10.43. Multiplied, that is about 21.3% a year. If your cash credit costs 11%, paying early with borrowed money still earns roughly 10 points, so the discount is worth taking whenever the limit has headroom. Note that this is the exact mirror of Lesson 3.1: what is expensive to offer as a seller is attractive to accept as a buyer.

body.title: The payment run
body.question: Cash is tight this week and you can fund only three of these four payments. Which one do you delay?
options: TDS deducted from last month's salaries, due on the 7th
A ₹6 lakh invoice from a micro enterprise, now 40 days old
A ₹9 lakh invoice from a large multinational supplier on agreed 60-day terms, due on the 48th day because of an early payment habit
PF contributions for last month, due on the 15th
body.explanation: Only the large supplier can be moved, and even then it is because you are paying ahead of agreed terms, so the real answer is to stop paying early rather than to pay late. TDS and PF carry statutory interest and penalties, and the micro enterprise invoice is approaching the 45-day limit that triggers interest and disallowance. Cash pressure never justifies delaying the two categories with legal consequences.

body.title: Fund the kiln by delaying everyone
body.scenario: Konkan Ceramics needs ₹1 crore for a new kiln. The bank limit is drawn and the promoter cannot add capital. In the management meeting, the plan proposed is simple: delay all supplier payments by 30 days for four months, collect the ₹1 crore from the float that creates, and buy the kiln outright. Purchases run at about ₹70 lakh a month, so the arithmetic appears to work.
body.prompt: What is wrong with this plan, and what would you propose instead?
body.modelAnswer:
Start with the arithmetic, because it does not even work.
1. Stretching payment by 30 days releases roughly one month of purchases, about ₹70 lakh, and it happens once. It is not ₹70 lakh a month for four months. After the first month the business is simply paying its bills 30 days later than before, and the float stops growing.
Now the real objections.
2. More than half those purchases are from micro and small suppliers. Delaying them past the statutory limit triggers compound interest at three times the bank rate, which is not tax deductible, and defers the tax deduction on the purchases themselves under Section 37(2)(g) of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Some of the "saved" cash comes straight back out as extra tax.
3. It shows up on a public filing. Amounts owed to micro and small suppliers beyond 45 days must be disclosed in MSME Form 1 and in the notes to the accounts.
4. It is a maturity mismatch. A kiln lasts fifteen years, so funding it with 30 days of supplier money means the loan is due long before the asset pays for itself. In month five, the suppliers want their money and the kiln cannot be sold.
5. Suppliers respond. Prices rise, priority falls during shortages, and the small fabricator who cannot fund 30 extra days may simply stop supplying.
What I would propose instead.
6. Fund a long-term asset with long-term money: a term loan or equipment finance over five to seven years, where the EMI is paid out of the extra production the kiln enables.
7. Ask the kiln vendor about staged payments tied to installation and commissioning milestones.
8. Use the working capital levers for working capital only: collect the ₹25 lakh sitting beyond 60 days from Lesson 3.1, negotiate longer terms with the large glaze supplier in writing, and clear slow-moving stock.
9. If the bank limit is genuinely exhausted, that is the conversation to have with the bank, and a funded kiln order with a clear payback is a far better case than a stretched payables position, which the bank will see in the stock statement anyway.

cards.definition: Amounts owed to suppliers for goods and services already received. Interest-free funding, within agreed terms.
Payment to a micro or small supplier within the agreed period, capped at 45 days, or 15 days without a written agreement.
Compound interest with monthly rests at three times the RBI bank rate on delayed payment to those suppliers.
That interest is not allowed as a deduction from income, so the buyer bears its full cost.
Carried over from Section 43B(h) of the 1961 Act. The purchase is deductible only in the year it is actually paid.
The buyer's bank pays suppliers early at the buyer's credit rating, while the buyer pays later.

points: Split payables into statutory dues, micro and small suppliers, and everyone else. Only the third group is negotiable.
Statutory dues are never a source of funding. Interest and penalties are automatic.
Paying a micro or small supplier beyond 45 days costs compound interest at three times the bank rate, gets no tax relief on that interest, and defers the deduction on the purchase itself.
Delays above 45 days are also disclosed publicly through MSME Form 1, filed twice a year.
Record every supplier's Udyam classification in the vendor master. Without it, no system can enforce the right terms.
Negotiate openly with large suppliers instead, offering volume, reliability or security, and consider supply chain finance so suppliers get paid early while you keep your terms.

body.text: Konkan Ceramics is fictional. The 6% bank rate, 25% tax rate and all interest figures are illustrative, not current rates. Statutory provisions are summarised for teaching and their application to specific suppliers, including traders, can be contested. Confirm the current position with your chartered accountant or legal adviser. This is not legal or tax advice.
